news.title: Jon Stewart Gets Big Laughs Blaming Haley Stevens for Anderson Cooper’s On-Air ‘Sass’
news.text:
“I mean, of course, we all knew there was drama in Michigan when Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in a contentious primary for the Democratic nomination,” Stewart said. “But Stevens has always been very clear as to their shared goal of defeating Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers.”

The “Daily Show” editors then cut to all the times Stevens denounced Rogers as a Donald Trump lackey. Nonetheless, on Sunday, Stevens revealed she’d be voting for Rogers – in a video that was awkwardly filmed at an angle.

“Is her car in a ditch?” Stewart quipped after watching the footage. “Is she endorsing Mike Rogers after getting in a car accident? ‘Real quick, before I lose consciousness, I am endorsing the nightmare.’”

As Stewart went on, he wondered aloud “what the f–k happened?,” adding that it was “the most diabolical episode of ‘Fargo’ I’ve ever seen.”

“What could have driven, somewhat erratically…” he joked, before seriously asking, “What could have driven Haley Stevens into the arms of the Rogers campaign?”

The show then cut to press conference footage of Stevens bemoaning the fact that she was left out of El-Sayed’s campaign.

“That says why you’re mad at Abdul. But not why you’re for Rogers,” Stewart countered. “Rogers is, hold on, let me find the word, a nightmare, who is against every principle you’ve worked for your entire career. I mean, at least say you were visited by three ghosts who convinced you that it turns out people don’t need health insurance. This can’t really be about getting your feelings hurt.”

Here’s where the “Daily Show” zeroed in on Stevens’ disastrous CNN interview with Cooper. In the footage, Cooper noted, “You wanted to be at a public event with him up until some point, I guess yesterday. It’s just an interesting change. And I think a lot of people are curious to try to understand it.”

As an uncomfortable silence filled the airwaves, Stevens commented, “Was that a question, Anderson, or…”

“No, I wanted to see if you wanted to fill in the silence, but you don’t,” Cooper hit back.

Stewart got a kick out of Cooper’s sassy on-air response, playfully wagging his finger as his studio audience broke out into laughter and applause. 

“Do you see what you just did there, Haley Stevens? Are you happy with yourself?” Stewart sounded off. “All that sass you made. You just turned Anderson Cooper into Andy Cohen. Is that what you wanted?”

After the crowd broke out into another round of laughter and applause, Stewart added: “He didn’t want to sass you. He’s a newsman. He doesn’t want to sass you. You gave him no choice but to sass.”

“The Daily Show” airs weeknights at 11 p.m. ET on Comedy Central.

news.title: Trump DOJ Targets 405 Ballots. Some May Belong to U.S. Citizens
news.text: The Department of Justice (DOJ) wants Washington state election officials to hold back the ballots of more than 400 voters it alleges are noncitizens—while its own letter concedes that some of those voters "may have subsequently naturalized." The 405 ballots the department wants set aside, in other words, could belong to U.S. citizens. On Monday, the day before Election Day, three civic and labor groups asked a federal judge in Seattle for an emergency order blocking the demand. Their lawsuit, filed Friday, argues the Trump administration has no legal power to tell a state which lawfully cast ballots to count. It also says the administration is using the threat of prosecution to frighten election workers and naturalized voters. Why It Matters States administer elections in the U.S., while federal prosecutors can investigate and charge people suspected of violating federal election laws. But in the final weeks of the 2026 midterms, the DOJ has tried something rarer: telling states, before the votes are counted, which ballots to set aside. Washington is the third state where the DOJ has gone to court or threatened to this fall over how votes are counted. In California, it sought to have ballots from more than 20,000 people it identified as likely noncitizens segregated; the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request Monday evening. In Alaska, it tried to block certification of the Senate race over a dispute about two candidates named Dan Sullivan, and a judge dismissed the case Sunday. So far, every court to rule in these cases has turned the government down. The groups say the risk falls hardest on naturalized citizens. Federal records may not reflect that a green-card holder later became a citizen, they argue, and Washington’s elections office has said the federal system that the DOJ relies on frequently flags legitimate U.S. citizens. The DOJ’s letter acknowledges the possibility in its own words. It does not say how many people on its list might be affected. What DOJ Demanded Pete Serrano, the top federal prosecutor in eastern Washington, signed the October 26 letter to Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and announced it alongside Neil Floyd, acting U.S. attorney in Seattle. It said the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had identified more than 400 people who were registered to vote in Washington despite not being citizens, and who had cast more than 1,500 ballots between them, some as recently as the August primary. It gave the state 24 hours to check the names and a deadline of noon October 28 to reply. The core request was blunt. If anyone on the list returned a ballot, county officials were not to verify the signature or count it until the person's citizenship was settled. If Washington did not comply, the letter warned, the United States "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief." The letter said only that the DHS had identified the names “through the efforts of our federal law enforcement partners.” Floyd offered more at the news conference. Agents, he said, had been questioning noncitizen detainees and people crossing the border about whether they had voted, then checking that against federal immigration databases and public voter rolls. “We are having to do this essentially one person at a time,” he said, according to KOMO. The letter also promised more. Prosecutors said they expected "imminently" to receive a second list and to send it before what they called the "November 2, 2026 General Election." Election Day is November 3. A List With Holes The sentence at the center of the case sits in the letter's own description of the people it names. They "are or were noncitizens," it says, before adding in parentheses: "they may have subsequently naturalized." Washington's review found more problems. In an October 28 reply, Hobbs said a preliminary check showed the list "includes United States citizens and is not reliable." The DOJ had sent a PDF of a printed spreadsheet rather than a data file. It left out voter identification numbers and addresses, which officials need to match a name to a registration. One record dated to 1994, his office said. A declaration from Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, cited in Monday’s court filing, puts numbers on the gaps. Federal prosecutors have publicly put the list at 405 names; the state counted 403 unique people on it. At least 62 of them had not been sent a ballot at all, because their registrations were canceled or inactive or the state could not find them. Floyd himself acknowledged limits. According to the complaint, which quotes a transcript of his news conference, he described the list as covering "a very tiny population of people that we have made contact with recently." He allowed that "there might be a lot of John Does." And he said some people on it had told agents they never filled out a ballot. The Lawsuit OneAmerica Votes and the Latino Community Fund of Washington State both work largely with immigrant and Latino voters. They sued October 30 in federal court in Seattle, joined by the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. Represented by Elias Law Group, they named President Donald Trump, the DOJ, DHS, Floyd and Serrano, among others. The groups argue that the Constitution leaves election administration to the states and that no federal law lets prosecutors order ballots held back. Many of their members are naturalized citizens who, the groups say, would never know their ballot had been set aside. On Monday, they asked U.S. District Judge Jamal N. Whitehead for an emergency order. As of Monday evening, no hearing had been publicly scheduled. What People Are Saying Newsweek asked the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Seattle on Monday whether the second list had been sent, whether the DOJ would oppose the emergency motion, what its next steps in Washington were and how it responded to the state’s findings. The office said it does not comment on pending litigation and does not expect to say more until after the election. It pointed instead to a statement Floyd issued Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed. In that statement, Floyd wrote that Washington is “knowingly sending out ballots to non-citizens and trusting that the non-citizens will not fill out the ballot.” Washington does not require documentary proof of citizenship to register; voters attest to it when they sign up. Abha Khanna, a partner at Elias Law Group, called the demand “unlawful intimidation of election officials, plain and simple.” What Happens Next Washington votes by mail, and ballots postmarked by Tuesday will be counted for days afterward, so the fight is likely to outlast Election Day. A ruling from Whitehead, the promised second list or a DOJ lawsuit against the state could all come during the count. news.title: Crude oil prices rebound amid fresh Middle East tensions, supply disruption concerns
news.text: Digital Desk | New Delhi, Nov 3 (IANS) Global crude oil prices on Tuesday rebounded in early hours after US forces reportedly had struck Iran's Qeshm Island, heightening concerns over a potential escalation in regional tensions and renewed threats to energy supplies from the Middle East. Brent crude -- the international oil benchmark -- rose 61 cents or 0.58 per cent to $105.38 a barrel. Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate crude gained 71 cents or 0.73 per cent to $97.17 a barrel in early trade. The rebound followed a sharp decline in the previous session when Brent settled $8.66 or 7.6 per cent lower at $104.77 a barrel. Reports -- citing US officials -- claim that American forces targeted Qeshm Island in an operation described by some officials as defensive to limit Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, market participants said the development prompted traders to reintroduce a geopolitical risk premium into crude prices. The latest military developments come even as diplomatic channels remain active. In addition, Tehran said discussions with Washington aimed at ending the conflict are continuing, although recent talks mediated by Qatar concluded without a breakthrough despite revised proposals from the Iranian side. US President Donald Trump also signalled uncertainty over the prospect of renewed military action, saying an agreement with Tehran remained possible and casting doubt on whether previously threatened strikes would proceed. The conflict which began in late February has significantly curtailed shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical energy corridor that traditionally handles roughly one-fifth of global crude oil and natural gas flows. The prolonged disruption has contributed to elevated fuel prices, adding pressure on the US administration as higher gasoline costs remain a concern for consumers and policymakers. Additionally, Brent crude closed October at its highest level in six months amid concerns that instability in the Middle East could intensify following the US midterm elections. In a separate development, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had delegated certain authorities to the government to pursue peace negotiations.

news.title: Fifa to share ‘key documents’ over World Cup sell-off plan
news.text:
Fifa says “key documents” relating to president Gianni Infantino’s failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors will be made available to members of its council – but access will be subject to “strict review protocols”.

Last month, Uefa gave football’s world governing body until 2 November to release details about the hugely controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer a list of questions relating to its governance and decision-making.

That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.

Just hours before the deadline from European football’s governing body passed, Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom wrote to members of its main decision-making body – saying they will be able to view “key documents”, but only in person at the organisation’s headquarters in Zurich.

In his letter – seen by BBC Sport – he says the paperwork will be available “under strict review protocols to preserve confidentiality”, with council members asked to register to see them within the next two weeks.

It is unclear which documents will be made available.

BBC Sport has been told Fifa viewed Uefa’s two-week deadline to respond to more than 100 questions as unfeasible, given their recent focus on organising a new youth World Cup in Azerbaijan and preparations for an extraordinary congress later this month.

Sources have also indicated Fifa’s ability to answer some questions is limited by legal action that Uefa launched in October in the US, requesting disclosure of evidence and documents, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

Last month, Uefa told Fifa that it had failed to address “a number of fundamental questions”.

The letter included eight pages of questions covering a number of issues, from FFE and funding to national associations, to the awarding of an inaugural Fifa Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

“The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of ‘potential governance reforms’ do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage,” the letter said.

“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”

Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline, but hoped it added to the pressure on Infantino before 18 November – the cut-off date for any candidates to confirm they are standing against him in next year’s presidential election.

In his letter Grafstrom says that Uefa’s demand “contains significantly more questions than the Fifa administration could reasonably have anticipated” and that it is “currently working on a response which we will share with all council members in due course.”

He adds that the FFE proposal “could not have proceeded without the cumulative and mandatory approval of the council, and a majority of member associations, and in that event, there would be and has been no penalty to Fifa for withdrawing from the proposal”.

news.title: North Korean leader's sister blasts FBI's crypto theft probe as 'political provocation'
news.text: Digital Desk | Seoul, Nov 3 (IANS) North Korea on Tuesday flatly dismissed the outcome of a US investigation that blamed Pyongyang for a massive cryptocurrency theft from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, calling it a "grave political provocation" against the North. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, made the remarks, referring to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) announcement Saturday that the regime is responsible for the theft of more than US$6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance. The FBI linked the theft to a North Korean hacking group it calls TraderTraitor, a name previously tied to other cryptocurrency heists. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said in a statement carried by the North's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). DPRK is short for the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." North Korea has been blamed for cyber thefts before and has denied any involvement. It is rare for Kim to issue a statement on a hacking incident. Kim called Washington's accusation a "sinister" attempt to damage the international image of North Korea and undermine its dignity and national prestige, as well as another grave violation of the sovereignty of the North in cyberspace. Turning the blame back on Washington, she said, "As soon as the present US administration took office last year, it announced that it would confiscate illegally stolen cryptocurrency assets and use them as a state's strategic reserve." Anyone who looks at who will end up with "the so-called stolen cryptocurrency" once it is retrieved, she said, "may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident." She said North Korea is "closely monitoring" a variety of what she called Washington's persistent provocations against it. "We have issues to reconsider in diverse aspects as regards the very unpleasant US hostile attitude," Kim warned. A senior official at South Korea's unification ministry noted it was Kim's first statement on accusations of North Korea's cyber hacking. "The North appears to be treating this matter seriously, as the international fallout from the Binance hacking incident grows, and has elevated its response", by speaking through Kim, the official said. In similar cases in the past, the North usually responded with a statement issued by its foreign ministry. Pyongyang appears to care about its international image as it seeks to be portrayed as a "normal state," the official added. The statement is regarded as an attempt to keep the North's cyber activities from becoming an international issue and to pressure the US to drop what Pyongyang calls a hostile policy toward it. The ministry finds it hard to "predict" what effects the hacking incident would have on a potential summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and US President Donald Trump. North Korea has remained unresponsive to Trump's repeated overtures to resume summit diplomacy.

news.title: Sad News For SA: US Has Announced To End South Africa’s AGOA Benefits From January 2027, Check Out
news.text:
The United States government has announced plans to terminate South Africa’s participation in the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a preferential trade programme that has provided eligible African countries with duty-free access to the American market for more than two decades.

The proposed termination is expected to take effect on 1 January 2027, potentially exposing South African exporters to higher tariffs and creating uncertainty for businesses that depend on trade with the United States.

US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer announced the decision on Monday, 2 November 2026, confirming that President Donald Trump had taken the step following an annual review of countries benefiting from the programme.

According to Greer, South Africa and Rwanda have been engaging in practices that Washington considers inconsistent with the eligibility requirements of AGOA. The United States has therefore notified Congress and the South African government of its intention to end South Africa’s participation in the programme.

In explaining the decision concerning South Africa, the US administration reportedly raised concerns about barriers to American trade and investment, corruption, national security and foreign policy.

The announcement represents a significant development in economic relations between Pretoria and Washington, particularly given the importance of the American market to several South African industries.

AGOA was introduced in 2000 to strengthen economic relations between the United States and eligible African countries by providing preferential access to the American market. The programme allows qualifying products from participating countries to enter the United States without certain import duties, creating opportunities for exporters and supporting trade-related employment.

South Africa has been among the programme’s major beneficiaries, using the preferential arrangements to export a wide range of products, including motor vehicles, agricultural goods, jewellery and ferroalloys.

Available trade figures indicate that South Africa exported approximately $1.7 billion worth of goods to the United States under AGOA in 2025, highlighting the potential economic implications of losing access to the arrangement.

If the proposed termination takes effect, South African businesses that currently benefit from duty-free access could face increased costs when exporting to the United States. The resulting changes could affect the competitiveness of certain products, particularly in industries that rely heavily on access to the American market.

The automotive and agricultural sectors could be among the industries closely monitoring developments, given their participation in South Africa’s exports to the United States.

The announcement also raises questions about the future direction of trade relations between the two countries and whether diplomatic or trade negotiations could take place before the proposed termination date.

For South Africa, the development presents a challenge for its exporters and policymakers, who may need to explore alternative markets, strengthen existing trade relationships and engage Washington over the concerns raised by the Trump administration.

Although the proposed termination is scheduled for January 2027, its broader implications will depend on subsequent diplomatic engagements, the implementation of the US decision and the extent to which affected industries can adjust to any changes in trade conditions.

The development is likely to remain an important issue in discussions surrounding South Africa’s international trade strategy and its economic relationship with the United States.

Donald Trump has dealt South Africa a major trade blow, with thousands of jobs potentially at risk. Here’s when the decision takes effect.

Image: X US President Donald Trump has moved to remove South Africa from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), threatening thousands of jobs in the country’s agricultural and manufacturing sectors.

The Trump administration announced on Monday, 2 November, that South Africa would lose its preferential trade benefits from 1 January 2027.

Rwanda also faces removal from the programme.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer confirmed that Trump had notified Congress and both governments of his intention to terminate their eligibility.

Washington accused South Africa of maintaining trade and investment barriers, corruption and policies it considers a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests.

The announcement follows months of strained relations between Pretoria and Washington.

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said government recognised the concerns raised by Washington’s announcement.

He said South Africa would accelerate efforts to find alternative export markets and protect jobs.

Government is pursuing opportunities across Africa, India, China and the European Union.

Tau maintained that although AGOA remained important, it did not represent the country’s entire economic relationship with the US.

According to government, approximately 89% of South African exports entered the American market under ordinary World Trade Organisation trading terms in 2025.

The decision has raised fears of job losses in agriculture and manufacturing.

Labour federation Cosatu warned that withdrawing South Africa’s trade benefits could place thousands of livelihoods at risk.

The citrus industry has also expressed concern about the impact on producers and workers, particularly in the Western and Northern Cape.

AGOA has allowed eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free since 2000.

South Africa has been one of the programme’s largest beneficiaries.

The latest move does not immediately end all trade between South Africa and the US. However, affected exporters could face additional tariffs when the country’s AGOA benefits expire at the end of December.

The announcement comes despite months of negotiations between South African officials and Washington aimed at preserving the country’s preferential trade access.

news.title: Negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the US to be held in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11
news.text:
Negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the US will be held in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. The time and place of the negotiations were announced on the social network X by US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Whitkoff, writes BBC.

According to him, the meeting will be dedicated to "post-war security measures, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps towards peace."

This week, American negotiators are expected to meet in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, Great Britain, the EU, and NATO to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe's post-war security architecture, and economic opportunities to support Ukraine's recovery, Whitkoff added.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg towards a comprehensive and lasting peace agreement that will ensure long-term security for future generations," wrote Donald Trump's special envoy.

In October, Whitkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, after which he traveled to St. Petersburg for negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The last negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, mediated by the US, took place in February this year — before the start of the US and Israel war against Iran.

news.title: Trump moves to end South Africa’s Agoa benefits, Pretoria pushes back
news.text:
Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau. Picture: Daniel Garzon/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images

The South African government has pushed back against Washington’s decision to terminate the country’s benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa), arguing that it made extensive efforts to address US concerns and accusing the United States of introducing new issues despite ongoing negotiations.

US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer on Monday announced that South Africa and Rwanda would be excluded from the duty-free trade programme from 1 January 2027, citing practices deemed inconsistent with Agoa’s eligibility requirements.

The decision follows a letter US President Donald Trump sent to President Cyril Ramaphosa in October, in which he accused Pretoria of failing to meet key Agoa requirements.

Trump said South Africa no longer meets the programme’s eligibility criteria, citing concerns over corruption, market access, and barriers to US trade and investment.

“The Government of South Africa has not established, or is not making continual progress toward establishing, a system to combat corruption and bribery or the elimination of barriers to United States trade and investment,” he said.

Trump also accused South Africa of maintaining trade restrictions that negatively affect American businesses.

“South Africa continues to maintain significant tariff and non-tariff barriers affecting United States trade and investment, including barriers involving agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections, and intellectual property,” he said.

He further raised concerns about South Africa’s foreign policy stance, warning that its relations with certain countries could undermine “United States national security and foreign policy”.

Despite the decision, Trump left the door open for South Africa to regain Agoa benefits if it addresses Washington’s concerns.

“I will continue to monitor whether the Government of South Africa is making progress in addressing these concerns and meeting Agoa’s eligibility requirements,” he said.

“It is my hope that your government will work closely with my administration to address these issues so that South Africa can once again become eligible for Agoa benefits.”

The US’ decision could affect exporters, businesses and workers linked to Agoa-supported industries.

Government acknowledged the concern the decision would cause and said it was working closely with affected sectors to assess the fallout and protect jobs.

“Government recognises the concern that this decision may create for workers, exporters, businesses and communities linked to Agoa-supported value chains,” said the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition.

The DTIC said the government had gone beyond the concessions offered in 2015 to preserve preferential access to the US market.

“Government has put extensive efforts to constructively respond to the US concerns and has tabled beyond the 2015 concessions, additional concessions through the appropriate channels.”

However, the DTIC expressed frustration over Washington’s latest position.

“It is, however, unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions as part of the negotiations process that commenced in 2025.”

Despite the setback, the government sought to reassure investors and businesses that Agoa represents only a small portion of South Africa’s overall trade.

According to the DTIC, about 89% of South African exports to the US entered the market under normal World Trade Organisation rules in 2025, while Agoa exports accounted for roughly 10% of exports to the US and about 1% of South Africa’s total global exports.

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said the decision should not define relations between the two countries.

“This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States. However, a solution depends on the willingness of both parties to find solutions.”

Tau said the government would continue supporting affected sectors, protecting jobs, and expanding export opportunities in markets across Africa, Europe, Asia, and Latin America as it works to reduce the impact of losing Agoa benefits.

US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III says South Africa’s removal was a “predictable and preventable” consequence of government policies, accusing Pretoria of failing to address concerns raised by Washington and warning that it must recognise the gravity of the situation.

Bozell said the decision to exclude South Africa was “regrettable.”

news.title: Gold holds biggest jump in two months on Iran peace-deal hopes
news.text:
Gold was steady, after jumping the most in two months on Monday as hopes of a breakthrough in US-Iran peace talks sent oil prices plunging and eased anxiety over accelerating inflation. 

Bullion traded around $3,950 an ounce, having climbed 1.9 per cent in the previous session. Oil was flat following a tumble of more than 7 per cent on Monday, after the Iranian president said his government has been granted more authority by the country’s supreme leader to pursue negotiations, and US President Donald Trump hinted at progress in the discussions. 

The Middle East war — now in its ninth month — has sent energy prices and inflation surging, putting pressure on central banks to raise borrowing costs, which is negative for gold as it doesn’t pay interest. 

The precious metal slumped 6.8 per cent in October, breaking decisively below the $4,000 an ounce threshold at the end of the month to hit a one-year low. It was caught up in a retreat from artificial intelligence last week, prompting investors to liquidate bullion holdings to cover losses elsewhere. That’s left gold vulnerable to further declines, as Asian tech stocks headed for more losses on Tuesday after a selloff in US chipmakers deepened. 

US voters head to the polls on Tuesday for the midterm elections. For gold, what matters is how the election shapes the fiscal narrative, said wealth manager Noah Holdings Ltd.

Gold is sensitive to US Treasury interventions in the bond market, the government’s reliance on short-term debt and the Federal Reserve’s ability to keep short-term interest rates in check, according to emailed comments from the company’s investment office. Whether the election result affects those scenarios could indirectly impact bullion prices, it said.

Spot gold was little changed at $3,944.23 an ounce as of 10:22 a.m. in Singapore. Silver was down 0.8 per cent at $50.23, after rising more than 3 per cent on Monday. Platinum edged higher, while palladium fell slightly. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was steady after falling 0.3 per cent over the previous two sessions.

news.title: MAGA Goons Fume as Trump Blows His Big Election Pitch
news.text:
Donald Trump’s advisers have revealed their anger at the senior president for blowing his final pitch to voters before the midterm elections.

Trump, 80, spoke at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday to end his national midterm tour. The senior president visited 20 states in 32 days in an attempt to salvage Republicans’ fortunes at the ballot box on Tuesday.

However, during Trump’s speech, the president spent the first 17 minutes going into graphic detail about his costly pool renovations. 

He claimed, “The pipes were very old and in bad shape,” and spoke in depth about how his changes to the draining system should result in less algae, despite the country being in the throes of a cost of living crisis.

“I mean, they’ve had years here where you couldn’t see any water,” Trump said. “It was just algae and it had a bad aroma, to put it mildly. A lot of bad things happened.”

Trump didn’t start discussing economic policies until 18 minutes into his speech, but within minutes, he had turned his attention to the previously “inferior” grass in front of the White House. “Now it’s beautiful,” Trump said.

Trump’s fixation on algae, grass and his plans to renovate other Washington monuments just hours before Americans were due to vote “frustrated Republicans,” according to the Wall Street Journal.

The report claimed that even some of Trump’s own advisers “privately expressed exasperation” that the president did not use his high-profile speech on election eve to “squarely focus on the economic issues that voters say they care most about.”

The Journal noted that GOP operatives in recent days, “Have grown increasingly worried that they will suffer far-reaching losses in this week’s election,” leading to a “dour” mood inside the White House.

A person close to Trump “texted a facepalm emoji,” when asked for a response to his pool-centric speech, the report said, while a prominent Republican strategist claims the president’s backdrop was great, but the message was wrong.

Another said that a repeat outbreak of algae in Trump’s beloved pool “would be the least of their problems,” should Republicans lose control of the House and the Senate on Tuesday.

Trump’s war with Iran has led to soaring gas prices, despite the president promising for months they would go down. He repeated that line Monday, stating, “Because we’re winning with Iran, easily winning.”

Trump returned to the pool 38 minutes into his speech, repeating, “The pipes have been just been changed. The whole thing is in great shape.” 

At the start of his speech, the president even said, “We’re giving serious thought to changing the name to the Trump Reflecting Pool. We’ll announce that sometime tomorrow,” before saying, “I’m kidding.”

Retiring Nebraska Republican Rep. Don Bacon told the Journal that Trump “has never been known for message discipline,” adding, “At least he wasn’t talking about men’s behinds.” Trump spoke about Republican Jon Husted’s rear end multiple times during his rally speeches.

After Trump had finished speaking, some of his advisers argued that the remarks weren’t intended to be a closing message for voters, the Journal’s report said.

However it noted a senior White House official previewed the speech to reporters on Sunday using those exact terms, and that Trump was making his final argument to voters and sharing his accomplishments in office.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said the content of Trump’s election eve speech on Monday demonstrated he had “lost the plot.”

Speaking to Anderson Cooper on 360°, Clinton said that in 2016, Trump “knew how he wanted to present himself,” and had “people around him who at least had some ability to rein him in or say ‘no’ to him.”

“He’s totally unfettered and unhinged now,” she said on Monday evening. “And for him to go to the Reflecting Pool, one of the great failures of his efforts to redo Washington and stand there as though it was a huge success... I mean, you can’t make this up. He is so focused on himself.”

She added, " I mean, he’s truly lost the plot of being president for the American people, of winning a midterm election.“

news.title: Florida jet crash witnesses describe boom, chaos after disaster
news.text:
A deadly business jet crash that killed all nine people aboard sent shockwaves through a South Florida community, leaving residents scrambling from their homes and wondering whether they had witnessed an attack.

The Learjet 60 crash occurred around 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 1 as the aircraft traveled from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, according to authorities. The jet went down near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, scattering debris, sparking fires and forcing the evacuation of hundreds of residents living near the impact site.

Videos captured the aircraft nosediving near a busy roadway and the entrance to a mobile home community before erupting into flames. Federal investigators are still working to determine what caused the jet to go down.

Witnesses described a thunderous boom that shook homes, briefly knocked out power and sent neighbors rushing outside. For Armando Perez, a nighttime truck driver, the disaster began with a blast so powerful it jolted him awake.

"I thought, 'is this freaking Iran?'" Perez told the USA TODAY Network's Palm Beach Post, describing a force that shook his body like a gigantic subwoofer. Moments later, he heard neighbors screaming outside.

Resident Doug Schram also heard what sounded like an explosion after noticing a plane flying unusually low overhead. The blast was so powerful that power went out at his home for about 10 seconds, he said.

Smell and heat from debris were 'oppressive'

Perez, his mother and stepfather were among hundreds of residents evacuated from a nearby mobile home park after the crash. Authorities transported displaced residents by Palm Tran buses to the Greenacres Community Center, where many remained on Nov. 2 while investigators processed the scene.

Perez said his family had only moments to gather essentials before leaving, grabbing two days' worth of clothing, passports, wallets, phones and a blanket for their 3-year-old Chihuahua, Chupita. Mobile home park residents were ordered to evacuate without their vehicles.

After hearing the boom, Perez walked outside and initially felt confused. "It was raining just a few minutes ago, but now it was sunny," he recalled.

Perez said he later concluded the aircraft appeared to have broken through storm clouds as it plunged toward the roadway. The rain then returned and fell on the smoldering wreckage.

He said he was able to get within a few dozen feet of the crash site before emergency crews secured the area. The smell and heat were "oppressive," Perez said, recalling the odor of jet fuel spreading through the neighborhood.

According to Perez, the debris damaged homes and vehicles in the area.

Graphics: Moment by moment, how a Learjet passenger plane crashed in Florida

'Did someone shoot a missile?'

Schram, who lives about a half mile from the crash site, said he heard an aircraft flying unusually low before a loud explosion rattled his neighborhood.

"God, did someone shoot a missile or drone over my house?" Schram recalled thinking, according to the Palm Beach Post.

When he rushed outside, a neighbor told him he had seen what appeared to be a "mushroom cloud of smoke and fire" rising near the crash site, Schram said.

The explosion was so loud that Scharm and his neighbor wondered whether it could have been a missile headed toward President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in nearby Palm Beach. Minutes later, they began hearing sirens approaching from miles away.

Neighbors running up the street told them it appeared a plane had crashed. Schram said he was shocked when he saw the crater left in the roadway.

news.title: Asian stocks fall after US losses, oil holds drop: Markets Wrap
news.text:
Asian stocks declined after a selloff in US chipmakers deepened, overshadowing a plunge in oil prices amid optimism over diplomatic progress toward ending the war in Iran.

The MSCI Asia Pacific gauge dropped 0.6 per cent, with South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index sliding more than 2 per cent. The decline came after a gauge of US chipmakers extended a three-day rout to 12 per cent while the Nasdaq 100 sank 10 per cent from its peak, entering a technical correction. In a sign that some investors are looking to buy the dip, US stock futures gained. Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

Chinese equities dropped even after the central bank said it will encourage financial institutions to make greater use of stock-support tools and optimize their terms as authorities seek to bolster market stability.

Brent crude slipped 0.2 per cent to $104.61 a barrel after slumping 7.6 per cent on Monday with the US and Iran signaling a willingness to pursue peace talks. The war and the upcoming US midterm elections continued to weigh on the outlook.

Iran’s president said his government had been granted more authority by the nation’s supreme leader to negotiate, while US President Donald Trump hinted at progress in talks. Still, simmering hostilities are keeping the market on edge.

Easing geopolitical tensions are lowering energy prices and inflation risks, yet the drop in crude has so far failed to revive appetite for technology shares as concerns over AI spending and stretched valuations persist.

“Lower oil should be a tailwind for tech, but the fact that stocks could not hold the open even with crude plunging shows how little conviction is left even after last week’s carnage,” said Dave Mazza, chief executive officer at Roundhill Financial.

Korea’s Kospi Index led declines in Asia, with the two chip giants Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. the biggest drags.

“Korea’s semiconductor-heavy market is back on the front line of the global AI trade’s repricing,” said Hebe Chen, market analyst at Vantage Global Prime. “The divergence on Wall Street, where tech heavyweights are losing ground even as broader market breadth improves, suggests investors are rotating away from crowded AI trades rather than abandoning equities altogether.”

Apple Inc.’s shares fell in late US trading after the company delivered a mixed outlook to investors in its first quarterly report under Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, with narrower profit margins overshadowing an upbeat sales forecast. Elsewhere, Anthropic PBC disclosed a twelve-fold increase in quarterly revenue while outlining plans to spend more than $895 billion in the coming years.

China Stimulus

China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 0.1 per cent amid skepticism over the latest market support measures from the authorities. The two liquidity-injection tools — a swap facility and relending operations to encourage more stock purchases— reappeared with some adjustments as authorities sought to bolster market stability and confidence.

Chinese shares have been mired in a slump since the summer, weighed down by a weak economy and doubts over AI earnings. Previous attempts to revive the market — including a round of buying by the so-called national team starting July, and regulatory guidance to curb selling last month — have fallen short. The CSI 300 benchmark fell 8.5 per cent in October in its worst month in more than a decade.

Elsewhere, a Bloomberg gauge of the dollar was little changed Tuesday, while US Treasury 10-year futures slipped 5/32. There’s no trading of cash Treasuries in Asia due to the holiday in Japan.

The economic calendar adds another potential catalyst for the markets. US manufacturing activity picked up in October, supported by the strongest increase in production in nearly five years, while investors are looking ahead to a series of labor-market reports.

US job openings data due Tuesday are expected to show that listings edged higher in September, while weekly jobless claims Thursday are seen remaining near historically low levels. Economists expect Friday’s payrolls report to show job growth more than doubled to 65,000 in October, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2 per cent.”

“It’s going to be an extremely interesting week in the markets,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “We’ll have political issues to decipher as well as geopolitical ones. And growing doubts about AI investment returns will likely matter much more than historical patterns in determining the market’s direction going forward.”

news.title: James Carville Makes Bold Election-Eve Prediction
news.text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville has delivered a sanguine prediction of how his party will fare in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The former Bill Clinton aide, 82, appeared on MS NOW’s The Beat with Ari Melber on Monday to give his final assessment ahead of the next day’s consequential elections.

Melber asked the legendary politico if he believed Tuesday is an “economy election.”

“It is, but it is a corruption election,” Carville explained. “I think people have tied corruption to the economy, so I want to be very clear. Corruption is a challenge, and every election is about the economy. It always has been. But I think the corruption issue is really kind of center stage.”

The longtime Democrat said he believes President Donald Trump’s vastly unpopular war on Iran will serve to “expose a lot of corruption” and that “there’s a lot we don’t know.”

“It’s highly likely that the Democrats are gonna control both houses of the Congress after the election tomorrow, and I think we’re going to be in for a lot more—we’re gonna find out a lot after January 6,” he added.

Melber pressed Carville on his prediction, asking him to clarify if he believes the Democrats will truly control both congressional chambers after the midterms.

“I’m not very good at predicting, but it’s hard to look at this and not walk away with the fact that, yes, they’re gonna win the House and win the Senate,” he asserted.

He continued, “Remember, all these previous elections since Trump was elected, Democrats have been overperforming by like eight to ten points. It’s no reason to believe that they won’t overperform by that level tomorrow, and if they do, it’s gonna bear a lot of fruit. I can’t tell you specifically which one and which not, but there’ll be some ripe pickings there.”

Melber then showed a graphic of the seven battleground Senate races where Democrats have a firm advantage, including Michigan, Texas, and Maine. The host asked Carville what he makes of the polling.

“What jumps out at me,” Carville said, “the most unlikely outcome is that, not impossible, is that it breaks five-five. These things tend to break one way, and, historically, to make you feel good, they generally break for the out-party.”

“I think that, like, South Carolina, Mississippi is highly competitive,” he continued. “I’ve never been able to really break through in people’s minds just how competitive Mississippi was.”

He added, “And the other race I would really—and not just because I’m a homer—I think the Louisiana Senate race is gonna come down to the wire. I really believe that.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House for comment.

news.title: Trump spends final day before midterms discussing Reflecting Pool makeover
news.text:
US President Donald Trump spent the day before Tuesday's midterm elections promoting renovations to Washington's Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, drawing criticism for focusing on construction projects rather than campaigning for Republicans.

According to the Associated Press, Trump displayed photographs of the pool's restoration during a speech on Monday, highlighting improvements to its water, landscaping and plumbing.

“That’s not grass, that’s algae,” Trump said while showing an image of the pool before renovations.

The project has faced problems, including algae growth and a peeling blue liner. Trump blamed vandalism, although the Justice Department previously acknowledged that rushed repairs caused the liner to detach.

Republican strategist Doug Heye criticised the president's priorities, calling the event the “last thing” Republican candidates needed before Election Day.

Trump also discussed plans for a triumphal arch, a public golf course and a National Garden of American Heroes.

After spending more than 20 minutes discussing renovations, Trump turned to the midterms, warning that Democrats posed a threat to the country.

He defended his administration's economic record and military action against Iran, while acknowledging that sitting presidents often struggle in midterm elections.

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot,” Trump said.

news.title: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island on eve of midterm elections
news.text:
WASHINGTON – The United States attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Nov. 2, conducting a defensive operation on the eve of the midterm elections, according to a U.S. official.

The attack was intended to prevent Iran from using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets in the region, the U.S. official said. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Nov. 2 that it shot down two U.S. military drones south of Qeshm Island, according to Tasnim, an Iranian news agency close to the IRGC.

The Pentagon referred questions to U.S. Central Command, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The strikes were first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

CENTCOM had not publicly disclosed any strikes against Iranian military targets since Sept. 1. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to downplay the extent of the fighting in the Middle East in the weeks leading up to the midterms.

Republican candidates across the country have struggled to overcome broad opposition to the Iran war among Americans. The conflict in the Middle East has upended the global economy and driven up fuel prices, contributing to voter concerns about affordability.

Speaking at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool earlier on Nov. 2, Trump said the Iran war is "not a war."

"I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months," he added. 

Iran war: US military cost tops $47B, Pentagon tells Congress

The strikes on Iranian military targets come as Vice President JD Vance has led a diplomatic effort to restart peace negotiations in the days before the midterms. Trump had repeatedly suggested he could restart major military operations against Iran after the election.

Vance told reporters on Nov. 2 that Washington has not set a deadline for Tehran to agree to a ceasefire and that Trump retains both military and non-military operations.

Vance said that he recently spoke with Trump about the state of the negotiations with Iran and that U.S. officials recently had several "good conversations with the Iranians."

"We’ve certainly made some progress," he added. "We’ll see if we can make some more."

news.title: Trump Says Alaska's ‘Two Dan Sullivans’ Ballot Is Confusing. Voters Agree?
news.text: Marvin Willard Jr. has never lived anywhere but Alaska. A Tlingit man from the Chilkat Valley and the village of Klukwan, he says he has followed this year's U.S. Senate race "fairly close"—close enough to know his ballot will carry two men named Dan Sullivan, and close enough to have decided that this is not what keeps him up at night. "I don't think there should even be an issue on that," Willard told Newsweek. What he wanted to talk about was the cost of living. "Why don't you raise money to offset our fuel costs in Alaska?" he asked of the candidates and the money pouring in behind them. "Why don't you raise money to offset all the food prices?" Whether voters can tell the two men apart is only half of what hangs over Tuesday's election. The other half is whether anyone tried to make it harder for them. That question is now the subject of federal and state criminal investigations, and it is at the center of a New York Times report alleging Democratic involvement in recruiting the second Sullivan, which Mary Peltola's campaign denies. The Alaskans who spoke with Newsweek in the race’s final days were divided on whether the ballot itself was easy to read. One also said that if anyone deliberately tried to mislead voters, it should be taken very seriously. The Ballot, Briefly President Donald Trump says the ballot is the problem. On October 25, he argued it should have called his endorsed candidate "Senator Dan Sullivan" rather than "incumbent," because "a lot of people don't know what incumbent means." As printed, it lists Dan S. Sullivan as a registered Republican and the incumbent, and a retired Petersburg schoolteacher as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party at all. In June, the state’s elections director disqualified the second Sullivan, determining that he had filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead.” Two Alaska courts overruled her, finding no state law requiring a candidate to run in good faith. In August's primary, the senator drew 41.4 percent of the vote and his namesake 2.5 percent. On Sunday, a federal judge dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he ordered, that sought to delay certification if the senator lost and the votes cast for his namesake could have changed the result. The department plans to appeal, and federal and state investigators are still at work. That is the version of the story the country has been following. The Alaskans who spoke to Newsweek were telling a different one. 'Opens Up for Mistakes' In Wasilla, where Trump rallied beside the senator in mid-October, Ronny Johansson gives his neighbors the benefit of the doubt. "Surely the majority of voters have the ability to make out the difference between the two Sullivans," he said. But he also saw the potential for confusion: "Having two similar names on the ballot definitely opens up for mistakes." In a race forecasters call a toss-up, a mistake doesn't have to be common to matter. Johansson refuses to let either party off the hook. "Stacking the ballots isn't new, and is a tactic that both parties have used before," he said. "But that doesn't diminish the seriousness of cheating and being fraudulent in elections. This is something that has to be taken very seriously and must be stopped." "The voters deserve truly honest elections," he said. "Therefore the system has to be changed." ‘Total Confusion’ For Henry Symons, the mistakes Johansson worries about aren’t hypothetical. “Yes, total confusion!” he said. Symons said he was voting early in Kenai when a friend realized they had marked the wrong Dan Sullivan. Election workers destroyed their ballot and gave them a new one. Symons added that he would have made the same mistake if his friend hadn’t warned the group. Newsweek could not independently confirm the account. The Alaskan also said he believed the situation was deliberate: “Totally a setup!" Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats deny any role in the second Sullivan’s candidacy, and investigators have not publicly named any targets. Innokenty Lestenkof has heard similar worries, especially from older voters. “I definitely agree it confuses people, especially the elderly,” he said. Several of his elderly friends, he said, asked him how they could be sure they were voting for the right Sullivan. His answer was the label Trump says too few people understand: “I said the one with incumbent next to him.” 'No One is Confused' Christy O'Brien rejects the premise outright. "No one is confused," she said. "Everyone knows there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. It has been on the news forever and is a non-issue." She points to August's results as her proof. "If people were confused, there would have been a more even split in the primary," she said, "but there wasn't an even split or anywhere even close to it." The general election will test that with a much larger electorate. About a quarter of Alaska’s registered voters cast ballots in the August primary, according to the Division of Elections, and general elections typically draw far more. 'Political Theater' Michelle Chase is an undeclared voter, one of the many Alaskans who don't belong to a party, and she says she votes for the person, not the label. "It's not a real concern," she said. "It was easy to distinguish between the two Dans on the ballot. The issue was already addressed by the courts in AK." What's left, as she sees it, is a performance. "It's just political theater at this point," she said. 'Everybody's Interested in Alaska' Willard traces his lineage to the Eagle Nest House in Sitka, and his view of the race starts with the land. "All of our resources took thousands of years to get this plush," he said. "We should be protecting it, because the longer you sit on plush real estate like Alaska, the more it's going to be worth in the future." He doubts that resource development, including the proposed natural-gas project, would leave enough behind for Alaskans. Its backers argue it would bring jobs and revenue. "If you want to benefit us," Willard said, "then give us 51% of the profits." He is just as skeptical of the national attention now trained on the state. He sees the fight over the ballot as an effort to sway votes, and he directed that criticism at both national figures and Alaska's own officeholders. He remembered a time when companies in the Lower 48 wouldn't even ship to Alaska. "Now all of a sudden everybody's interested in Alaska," he said. Investigators and Senator Sullivan's campaign treat the recruitment allegations as a serious question about whether voters were deliberately misled, and those inquiries are still open. Willard's frustration is broader. "There's candidates that tell you what they're going to do for Alaska," he said, "and there's candidates that point the other finger." Too many, he believes, avoid specifics for a reason: "They don't want to be held accountable." 'Yeah, the Truth' Asked what people outside Alaska might be missing, Willard answered in three words. "Yeah, the truth." His advice for voters was just as short: "Stay off social media. Don't believe everything you see." The campaign emails filling his inbox tell him how much his children are worth. "Well, my kids should have been worth that much to begin with," he said. Johansson said the system has to change. Chase said the courts had already settled the matter. O'Brien said the primary results spoke for themselves. Willard asked why the money pouring into the race isn't going toward what Alaskans pay for fuel and food. On the narrow question of the ballot itself, they split. O’Brien, Chase and Willard said Alaskans can tell the two men apart. Symons and Lestenkof said some cannot. Johansson said most can, but that the ballot leaves room for mistakes. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: With two Dan Sullivans on the Senate ballot, Alaska voters weigh in on whether that’s a real problem.

There is a familiar rhythm to South Africa’s public conversation: a serious development becomes a looming catastrophe before we have even established precisely what is changing, who will be affected and what can be done. 

The confirmation that South Africa’s continued participation in the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) will end deserves urgent attention, obviously.

Exporters needed clarity, and workers whose livelihoods depend on American orders had every reason to be concerned. But the tone surrounding South Africa’s place in Agoa sounded like a “countdown to disaster” and inadequately described the position of a diversified economy with substantial commercial relationships worldwide.

There is a big difference between concentrated sectoral damage and an economy-wide disaster, and this should be articulated clearly.

Exclusion from Agoa alters the terms on which qualifying South African products enter the United States. It would not prohibit trade, cancel every commercial relationship or automatically render every exporter uncompetitive. 

The United States Trade Representative puts American goods imports from South Africa at $16.5-billion in 2025. That figure describes the wider goods relationship. It is not a measure of exports receiving Agoa preferences, still less an estimate of the losses that exclusion would cause. 

South Africa has made its case. The immediate question is how it should respond now that Washington’s decision is confirmed, and what kind of relationship it should seek to build.

The adverse decision warrants disappointment and a frank assessment of its consequences. Government also has an obligation to explain precisely what has changed. Which preferences have been withdrawn? When does the decision take effect? What additional costs will exporters face, and where are jobs most exposed? These answers should have shaped the public conversation before sweeping predictions of economic collapse take hold.

Publish a credible assessment of the actual exposure, developed jointly with industry and labour. The value of goods exported to America cannot simply be presented as the value of trade that will disappear. Some exporters may remain competitive; others may face substantial losses. A useful assessment must distinguish between them and identify the communities where intervention is most urgent.

Establish a targeted adjustment programme for viable businesses and affected workers. Depending on demonstrated need, this could include temporary working-capital support, assistance with export certification, help finding new buyers and measures to retain scarce skills. Assistance should have clear conditions, time limits and a realistic prospect of preserving production and employment. Government cannot promise to absorb every commercial loss.

Make diversification an operational programme. Telling a citrus grower or component manufacturer to “look elsewhere” is easy. Securing regulatory approval, negotiating supply contracts and getting goods to customers at a competitive price takes work. Government should agree sector-specific plans with exporters, assigning responsibility for removing particular barriers and reporting publicly on progress. African markets deserve sustained investment, alongside opportunities elsewhere, without pretending that any destination can immediately replace American demand.

Treat domestic reform as part of the response to the external shock. Every avoidable delay at a port, unreliable rail connection or unnecessary regulatory cost weakens an exporter’s ability to adjust. South Africa has limited control over decisions taken in Washington, but it has direct responsibility for the conditions under which its own firms produce and trade. Commitments on logistics, electricity and administrative efficiency should therefore become measurable components of the adjustment plan.

The longer-term task is to develop a framework for US-South Africa relations that can withstand political disagreement. It is difficult under the current resident on Pennsylvania Avenue, whose preferred style of engagement is vulgarity, threats and demands. He also has trouble concentrating and engaging with the boring, laborious aspects of governance. There is also the headache of the expected midterm election bloodbath. Donald Trump is not going to be in a good mood. Still, South Africa must stay the course.

Agoa has been valuable, but South Africa needs greater predictability than an annual eligibility decision can provide. Pretoria should set out its objectives for a more durable commercial relationship: clearer market-access arrangements, workable processes for resolving disputes and sustained cooperation on investment and productive capacity

There is room to begin with narrower, practical cooperation where both countries see value. Potential areas include energy, agricultural trade, advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure and research.

Each initiative should identify a concrete commercial or developmental objective, the institutions responsible and a way to measure delivery. Announcing another dialogue will achieve little unless it resolves problems or enables investment.

South Africa should continue engaging American companies, universities, investors and other institutions whose interests extend beyond the dispute of the moment. Those relationships have value in their own right and can sustain cooperation through difficult periods between governments.

None of this requires South Africa to pretend that the two countries possess equal economic power. It requires an accurate understanding of South Africa’s own assets, vulnerabilities and choices. 

Monday’s decision is adverse; the government’s credibility will depend on the quality of its response. It should explain the damage honestly, support those most exposed and give businesses a practical account of what happens next. It should also articulate a future relationship with the United States that recognises mutual commercial interests while allowing space for political differences. DM

news.title: Rubio speaks to Venezuelan minister about reforms that lay groundwork for elections
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with his Venezuelan counterpart on Monday about reforms that lay ​the groundwork for future free and fair elections in the ‌South American country, the State Department said in a statement.

Rubio met Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco at the State Department on Monday.

“The two discussed progress in the Venezuelan-led ​reconciliation talks, including institutional reforms that lay the groundwork for free, ​fair, and credible elections,” the State Department said in a ⁠statement.

Rubio said last week Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections ​and must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held.

In ​early January, President Donald Trump ordered a deadly US military raid in Venezuela that led to the seizure of ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, who were subsequently ​brought to New York to face trial.

Trump has since praised Maduro’s former ​vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who became interim president and began governing the country under ‌US ⁠oversight.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said last week Washington has suggested the country hold presidential elections next year.The Trump administration supports negotiations between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups, which do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement, ​on overhauling Venezuela’s electoral ​council and top ⁠court before the next elections.

Rodriguez’s interim government has signed deals with a variety of companies interested in oil ​and gas with support from Washington.

The US Treasury Department ​said on ⁠Monday the Venezuelan foreign minister also met US Treasury chief Scott Bessent, with Bessent discussing boosting energy production and getting investments into Venezuela.

The UN human rights ⁠office ​said in January that US intervention in Venezuela violated ​international law, while human rights advocates say Trump’s focus on exploiting Venezuelan oil echoes an imperialist ​approach.

news.title: Pregnant Savannah Chrisley reveals sex of 1st baby with much-older fraudster husband
news.text:
Savannah Chrisley and her husband, Jason Galanis, are having a baby boy.

The “Chrisley Knows Best” star announced she will be a boy mom in an Instagram reel posted Monday.

The reel presented cutting a cake with blue frosting inside, the couple happily kissing, and Chrisley’s parents, Todd and Julie, beaming and showing blue baby clothing and baby toys to the camera. 

“My sweet miracle boy… you are everything we prayed for and more. The most beautiful reminder that God’s plans are always greater than our own,” Savannah captioned the video.

“The past few days have reminded me just how cruel this world can be. But no amount of hate could ever overshadow the joy of loving you. You are a MIRACLE.”

“My precious baby boy, your daddy and I will spend the rest of our lives protecting you, praying over you, and loving you beyond measure. We may not be able to shield you from every bit of darkness in this world, but we promise to raise you to be a LIGHT in it,” she continued. 

“You are already our greatest blessing, our answered prayer, and the sweetest chapter of our lives. God knew exactly what He was doing when He gave us YOU. WE GET TO BE YOUR MOMMY AND DADDY!!!” she concluded.

The news comes after Chrisley, 29, revealed on Oct. 27 that she is engaged and expecting their first child, It was subsequently revealed that her fiancé is convicted fraudster Galanis, 56, and that she and Galanis secretly tied the knot on July 14 at a Baptist church in the Cayman Islands, months before publicly announcing their engagement and pregnancy.

Taking to Instagram with an intimate video of her and Galanis celebrating their upcoming arrival, the 29-year-old said, “I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine. 🥹🤍.

“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever… if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again,” Chrisley continued in the caption.

She said God sent her Galanis n the middle of “heartbreak” and that he helped her “heal.”

Chrisley called her husband her “protector” and “fiercest fighter,” as well as her “most loyal person.”

“My safe place. A man with the patience of Job (and Lord knows he needs it 🤣). The one who makes me laugh even on my hardest days,” the Good Girl Rx owner continued.

“For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you,” she wrote, along with an emoji of an engagement ring.

She then praised how supportive Galanis has been throughout her pregnancy so far, sharing that he has been to every doctor’s appointment and constantly gushes over her “beautiful” bump.

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words,” she wrote. 

“From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him,” Chrisley added.

In an accompanying episode of her “Unlocked” podcast, she shared more details about her new relationship, explaining that she met Galanis in the “world of politics” while she was campaigning for President Donald Trump to pardon her formerly imprisoned parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley.

She said that the two got engaged in December 2025, just five months after meeting, while vacationing in the Cayman Islands.

“When he gave me the ring, he was like, ‘Before I open this, I just want you to know that this is just an expression of love to you. This can be whatever you want it to be. This can be an engagement ring, a promise ring, a cocktail ring for all I care. I just want you to know how much I love you,’” she recalled.

Chrisley added that he did not put any “pressure” on her to accept the glittering diamond as an engagement ring.

“It happened really quick but it’s it is what it is right like timing means nothing,” she said. 

“That proposal was just right. It was everything I’ve always said.”

news.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
news.text:
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count. 

The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state. 

Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate. 

The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term. 

The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction. 

"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.

Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots. 

California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.
news.summary: The ruling, which comes on the eve of the midterm elections, essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots in the state.

news.title: CNN Host Roasts Trump Over Bonkers Final Election Pitch
news.text:
A stunned Kasie Hunt has ripped into Donald Trump’s baffling last-ditch plea to voters. 

On Monday’s The Arena, the 41-year-old anchor aired footage of the 80-year-old president’s election-eve speech at the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. 

“This is a massive piece of, piece of... pool,” Trump, 80, said in one of the supercuts aired on CNN, gesturing to the costly refurbished Lincoln pool. 

CNN cut back to Hunt, who could not contain her bewilderment.

“A massive, massive piece of pool,” she said, appearing to hold back a laugh.

“Did you catch the midterm message there?” she added, raising her hands.

“Because the president of the United States of America spent the first 22 minutes of his closing speech the day before Election Day talking about a massive piece of pool and grass and pipes and columns.”

Trump was back at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday to declare the renovation done, 203 days after he first vowed to paint the landmark “American Flag Blue.” In front of a handpicked crowd of National Park Service staff and Interior Department officials, he floated slapping his own name on it.

“We are giving serious thought to changing the name to the Trump reflecting pool,” he said, before adding, “I’m only kidding!”

But the president did not stop there.

“Later on in this address, he even talked about his arch and his golf course and his sculpture garden,” noted Hunt.

When he finally got to the midterm vote, he predicted a blowout win for the GOP. But then he hedged. 

“If the people that voted for me... go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” he said. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is... the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

Hunt, looking amused, took aim. “Well, there’s the closing message,” Hunt said, looking amused: “We gave it a shot.”

Pointing to the handful of attendees scattered across the memorial’s steps, Hunt said, “Laughing aside, it tells us so much.”

“That’s the size of the event,” she added.

“That’s the size of the event that the president used to try to end his midterm campaign. It’s in front of a pet construction project that, let’s be real, the team he hired botched,” Hunt said. She also pointed out that gas is now above $4 a gallon nationwide. AAA put Monday’s national average at $4.17. The Washington Post noted that’s the highest Election Day average on record.

“Trump was not in a battleground state alongside a Senate candidate. He was not at a big energetic MAGA rally,” she said. 

“Instead, it was just a man in there somewhere standing in front of a pool, asking you to love it,” Hunt said, riffing on Julia Roberts’ famous line from Notting Hill. 

The pool is just one of Trump’s pet home renovation projects around the capital, alongside his arch, golf course, and sculpture garden. 

When he drained the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in April, it came with big promises. He promised to plug the leaks, slap on a fresh coat of “American Flag Blue,” and wrap it up in a few weeks for just under $2 million.

But the big promises turned into an even bigger price tag. 

The gig went to a contractor who never had to bid, and the bill swelled to nearly $20 million. The fancy new liner peeled, and the algae came surging back. 

Trump blamed so-called “vandals,” going after former Olympian David Hearn. 

But the case sank when U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro dropped it, when prosecutors found the contractor’s slapdash rush job, not sabotage, was to blame.

But Trump refuses to let go of the vandal theory.

“The vandals went to work, but we went to work on the vandals,” he told the crowd Monday. “A lot of people tried to protect the vandals—but we got it done.”

The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment.

On Monday’s The Arena, the 41-year-old anchor aired footage of the 80-year-old president’s election-eve speech at the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. 

“This is a massive piece of, piece of... pool,” Trump, 80, said in one of the supercuts aired on CNN, gesturing to the costly refurbished Lincoln pool.

news.title: Democrats Could Have an Historic Midterm
news.text:
