news.title: Supreme Court blocks Trump administration's attempt to set aside California votes
news.text:
The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected the US President Donald Trump administration's emergency request to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots in California over claims that some voters may not be US citizens.

According to the Associated Press, the administration had identified approximately 20,000 registered voters it believed were likely noncitizens and wanted their ballots separated until their citizenship status could be verified.

The Supreme Court dismissed the request just hours after it was filed, delivering another legal setback to Trump's efforts to intervene in state election procedures.

California officials opposed the move, arguing that the administration's list contained numerous errors and that setting aside the ballots could prevent eligible citizens from having their votes counted.

The ruling comes ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, with Democrats hoping to gain greater control of Congress and increase scrutiny of the Trump administration.

The decision also follows an earlier Supreme Court ruling in September that rejected Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting nationwide.

The latest decision leaves California's existing ballot procedures in place as voters prepare for the November 3 elections.

news.title: Pretend I'm on ballot: Trump makes five-state push ahead of US midterms
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 3 (IANS) US President Donald Trump urged supporters across five states to vote Republican in the midterm elections, using a series of telephone rallies to cast congressional and governor’s races as a verdict on his presidency and the future of his agenda. In calls aimed at Georgia, Indiana, South Carolina, Alaska and New York, Trump backed candidates, attacked Democratic opponents and warned that his tax and border policies could be reversed if Republicans lost ground. His recurring message was personal: supporters should vote as though his own name appeared on the ballot. “So get out and vote tomorrow and pretend I'm on the ballot,” Trump told the South Carolina call. Taxes, immigration and gun rights featured prominently, while Trump highlighted energy projects in Alaska and tax deductions in New York. He repeatedly claimed his presence on a ballot produced a sharp increase in votes. The supplied transcripts offered no supporting data for that assertion. In Georgia, Trump urged voters to send Mike Collins to the Senate and elect Rick Jackson governor. He criticised Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and argued that Republican victories were needed to preserve his administration’s policies. In Indiana, Trump endorsed Victoria Spartz in the fifth Congressional District, praising her support for his tax and border agenda. He also credited her with helping secure more than $200 million for rural healthcare facilities. Trump attacked her Democratic opponent, JD Ford, over taxes, immigration and gun policy. The supplied material contains no response from Ford. In South Carolina, Trump backed Darline Graham for the Senate and Alan Wilson for governor. He praised Wilson’s record as attorney general and said Wilson would eliminate the state income tax if elected. Trump depicted Democratic candidates as threats to gun ownership and border enforcement. He also made accusations about their positions on transgender healthcare, often using insulting language. In Alaska, Trump urged voters to re-elect Senator Dan Sullivan and Congressman Nick Begich and support Bernadette Wilson for governor. He repeatedly distinguished the incumbent Sullivan from another candidate he said had the same name. He alleged an effort to confuse voters. Trump also urged voters to support a ballot measure that he described as ending ranked-choice voting. He credited Sullivan and Begich with advancing oil, gas and infrastructure projects. In New York, Trump backed Mike Lawler, Mike LiPetri and Jeanine Driscoll for Congress. He singled out Lawler’s work on the federal deduction for state and local taxes, known as SALT. “So, get out and vote for Mike Lawler, Mike LiPetri, and Jeanine Driscoll. They're fantastic people,” he said. Trump also defended military action against Iran during the New York call and predicted lower oil prices once the confrontation was resolved. The remarks provided no independent support for that forecast. US midterm elections take place halfway through a president’s four-year term. All 435 voting seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one-third of Senate seats are contested, alongside state and local offices. Presidents do not appear on the midterm ballot.

news.title: 26 Killed As Russia Strikes Ukraine Aid Centre, US-Brokered Talks Planned In Abu Dhabi
news.text:
This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of the latest developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, November 2. 
At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center in Zaporizhzhia region
Russia, Ukraine hit by cyberattacks after humanitarian truce ends in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Zelenskyy offers to stop hitting Russian refineries if the US delivers Patriot missiles
Multinational force to hold first excersise in Poland
A force of about 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will hold the first exercise of a new multinational force in support of Ukraine, the UK and France said.
The force is only to be deployed in the case of a ceasefire that would end the war between Kyiv and Moscow, with its aim being supporting Ukraine's army in securing the country.
"The exercise will allow the testing of the speed and efficiency at which several nations can deploy forces on land, sea and air to support Ukraine once hostilities have finished," a joint statement by the two countries reads.
With Russia not showing any intention of agreeing peace, the move could further antagonize Moscow.
The exercise will take place between November 9 and 22 in Poland, not far from the country's Ukraine border.
Russian, Ukrainian representatives to meet in Abu Dhabi — Witkoff
A trilateral meeting between officials from the US, Russia and Ukraine will take place in Abu Dhabi next week, US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff said.
According to Witkoff, the US will mediate "working-level" negotiations between Russia and Ukraine on November 10 and 11, in a bid of "advancing President Trump's mission to end the war."
"Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace," Witkoff posted on his X account, adding that meetings will also take place with representatives from NATO, Germany, the UK and the EU.
The goal, Witkoff said, is a "comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come."
Meanwhile, a senior US official told Reuters that Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the lead U.S. negotiators, are expected to represent the US in Abu Dhabi.
Zaporizhzhia: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center
At least 26 people were killed and five more injured on Monday when the Russian air force launched repeated strikes on a school which was functioning as an aid distribution center in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia.
The multiple attacks, in which Russian planes reportedly launched more than 10 glide bombs, took place in the village of Komyshuvakha, about 35 kilometers (31 miles) east of the city of Zaporizhzhia and a dozen kilometers away from the frontline.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attacks as "utterly horrific" and accused Russia of being well aware of the humanitarian purpose of the site.
"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on social media.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that every week, local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid at that very location."
Ukrainian emergency services said two ‌members of ⁠a ⁠rescue crew were among the dead after falling victim to the so-called "double-tap" strike in which a location is targeted again with the aim of hitting first responders.
The attacks came less than 24 hours after a localized six-day humanitarian ceasefire in and around the town of Oleshky in the neighboring region of Kherson had expired.
Zelenskyy said the temporary truce could potentially have led to further steps toward a possible deal to end the ongoing Russian invasion, but said after Monday's strikes:
"This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of ​de-escalation or any real justice... With these killings, Russia has sent a completely opposite signal; Russia is counting on further killings."
The Zaporizhzhia region has been targeted repeatedly for months by heavy Russian airstrikes.
Ukraine says Russia used ceasefire to rearm, rotate troops, Kremlin says 'it's normal practice'
Ukraine's General Staff on Monday blasted Russia's actions during a six-day humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, saying the Kremlin had used the break in fighting to rearm its forces and rotate troops in the front-line area.
In a social media post on X, the General Staff wrote: "Defense Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," adding, "The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."
Residents in the Kherson region were warned to be vigilant and told to pay attention to air raid sirens, noting that an intensification of attacks was to be expected after Russia used the brief pause to "strengthen its capabilities."
In Moscow, the Kremlin brushed off the critique, saying Ukraine, "could have used the ceasefire to re-group as well," calling such activity, "normal practice."
Kyiv region sees emergency power outages
Ukraine energy provider DTEK on Monday said that emergency power cuts had been initiated in Kyiv and the surrounding region at the request of national grid operator Ukrenergo.
The outages follow Russian attacks in central Ukraine that left over 200,000 Ukrainians in the area without power over the weekend.
DTEK had previously announced that, "equipment in the region has been seriously damaged due to enemy attacks," adding that energy workers were trying to "restore power to critical infrastructure facilities."
The attacks follow the Kremlin's playbook of seeking to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure, especially in cold months, in an attempt to break the will of Ukraine's citizens defending themselves against Russia's invasion by "weaponizing winter."
Ukraine says it evacuated more than 150 from Kherson region before ceasefire expired
Ukraine's military has said that about 170 people were evacuated from the Kherson region (news agencies cite numbers ranging from 167 to 180) before a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired at midnight (Moscow time, 2100 GMT) on Sunday.
No resumption of hostilities was immediately reported after what was the longest pause in fighting since Russian forces invaded in 2022.
Kherson's regional governor on Sunday urged residents remaining behind to avoid "red zones" where he said the threat of Russian strikes "remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
Kherson has been subjected to drones attacks, shelling, glide bombs and airdropped mines for nearly five years.
In all, nearly 800 people were reportedly evacuated from the region during the temporary ceasefire, with residents shuttled to Russian-annexed Crimea, then to the Russia town of Anapa, before being flown to Belarus and then Ukraine.
Among those evacuated were 22 children and 21 individuals requiring mobility assistance said Ukraine's army.
US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV — both of whom were reportedly involved in securing the pause in fighting — praised cooperation between the sides, voicing hope that such work might lay the groundwork for a broader peace.
Before Russia launched its illegal invasion on February 24, 2022, and took control of 70% of Kherson, the area was home to more than one million people. Now it is estimated that about 140,000 remain.
Russia hits military facility, cargo vessel, in Ukraine's Odesa
Russia's forces struck a military facility in Ukraine's Odesa region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Telegram on Monday.
The statement added that a cargo vessel, which the ministry claimed was used for military purposes, was also hit 58 kilometers (36 ‌ miles) south of ‌the Black ​Sea port city of Odesa.
Separately, news agency Reuters cited an official in Odesa as saying that four people had been injured in a Russian attack.
US reportedly pushing to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine
The United States is backing a ‌quick resumption ⁠of ⁠Russian natural gas ​exports to Europe ​via pipelines crossing ​Ukraine as part of talks ‌aimed at ‌securing ​an energy ceasefire before winter, the ​Wall Street Journal reported on ⁠Sunday, ​citing ​US, European ​and Ukrainian ‌officials.
The proposal involves selling Russian gas via a US intermediary to circumvent European sanctions, the report said, adding that it was mooted by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September.
DW could not ​immediately ⁠verify the report.
Russia's share in European gas supply has declined to about 11% now from 45% on the eve of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The European Union currently aims to completely phase out Russian gas imports by the end of 2027. And EU leaders have said they don't want to go back to relying on Russia for energy supplies.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine will stop refinery strikes if US sends Patriot missiles
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.
Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News, Zelenskyy said he had had "different and several" conversations with Trump and his team on the issue.
"We asked that we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he said.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid," Zelenskyy added.
The Ukrainian leader said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period.
Asked if he was concerned that this would be seen as trying to "leverage" Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."
Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles were dwindling.
Ukraine, Russia report separate hacking attacks
Emergency alert apps in both Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, officials said.
Ukraine's air force said an air raid alert app was hacked late on Sunday, with fake alerts being sent to smartphones, warning people of nuclear and chemical threats.
SPRAVDI, Ukraine's Center for Strategic Communications, blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
Hours later, Moscow said the mobile app of the Russian Emergencies Ministry was hit by "a massive cyberattack."
"Attention! The mobile application of the Ministry of Emergencies of Russia has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, enabling attackers to send false information to the public," the Emergencies Ministry posted on Telegram.
It said authorities were working to fix the issue.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the latest developments in Russia's war against Ukraine.
As a temporary ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town Oleshky ended on Sunday night, Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would stop targeting Russian refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's air force said it suspected the country's aid raid alert system had been hacked.
Russia's Emergencies Ministry, for its part, said that a "massive cyberattack" hit its application that is designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

news.title: North Korea denies involvement in Binance hack and criticizes FBI probe as 'a trite provocation'
news.text: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea on Tuesday denied its involvement in the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance, dismissing as 'a trite provocation” a US announcement that North Korean hackers were behind the incident.Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement 'a trite provocation” and 'an absurd rhetoric.''This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.'On this occasion, we confirmed Washington’s hostile attitude toward the DPRK once again and are closely monitoring a variety of persistent provocations of the U.S. against our state,” Kim Yo Jong said.Outside experts say North Korea has increasingly turned to cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency, helping sustain its struggling economy and fund its nuclear program in the face of stringent U.S.-led international sanctions and other challenges. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency estimated that North Korean hackers had stolen 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the previous five years.Although the country has mostly denied involvement, North Korea has been linked to numerous major cyberattacks in past years, including a 2013 campaign that paralyzed the servers of South Korean financial institutions, the 2014 hacking of Sony Pictures, and the WannaCry malware attack of 2017.South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that North Korea’s illicit cyber activities pose an increasing threat to the global digital economy and that Seoul was closely cooperating with the United States and the broader international community to address the threat.The Binance heist came as North Korea has ramped up its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after U.S. President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. On Tuesday, North Korea said it tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles.Asked by reporters later during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, Trump suggested investigators weren’t yet certain that North Korea was involved.'I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it,” Trump said of the case. 'We don’t know if it’s North Korea,” he added, though saying investigators could still determine that it was.In her Tuesday statement, Kim Yo Jong said: 'We have issues to reconsider in diverse aspects as regards the very unpleasant U.S. hostile attitude.”

news.title: White House Lists India Among Trade Deals 'Secured' By Trump
news.text:
Washington: The White House has listed India among the countries with which President Donald Trump "secured new and improved trade agreements", even though the interim trade agreement the two sides announced in February has not yet been signed.
The claim appears in a document titled "President Trump's Second Term: Promises Made, Promises Kept, Results Delivered", posted on the White House website on Monday, the last day of campaigning before Tuesday's midterm elections. The document lists what it calls 127 promises Trump has kept.
"By using tariffs as leverage, President Trump secured new and improved trade agreements with major U.S. trading partners covering more than half of global GDP - including the United Kingdom, European Union, Japan, China, India, Republic of Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Cambodia," the document said.
The word India in the White House list links to a February fact sheet headlined "The United States and India Announce Historic Trade Deal".
However, the joint statement the two governments issued on February 6 announced only a framework. "The United States of America (United States) and India are pleased to announce that they have reached a framework for an Interim Agreement regarding reciprocal and mutually beneficial trade (Interim Agreement)," it said.
The statement added: "The United States and India will promptly implement this framework and work towards finalising the Interim Agreement with a view to concluding a mutually beneficial BTA consistent with the roadmap agreed in the Terms of Reference."
Under the framework, India was to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and a range of US farm products, while Washington set an 18 per cent reciprocal tariff on Indian goods. The US also agreed to remove the reciprocal tariff on goods such as generic pharmaceuticals, gems and diamonds and aircraft parts, "subject to the successful conclusion of the Interim Agreement".
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on October 15 that the first tranche had been "finalised" and was going through legal drafting. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said the same day that the deal would be signed and implemented after legal vetting, without giving a date.
The 127-item list was released as Republicans fight to keep control of both chambers of Congress. It covers immigration, the economy, energy and foreign policy.

news.title: Asian stocks retreat ahead of US midterms, oil steadies
news.text:
SINGAPORE: Stocks edged lower at the start of Asian trade on Tuesday and oil prices stabilised after the previous session’s tumble, with ‌investors on edge ahead of the start of voting for the US midterm elections.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.9%, led by a decline of as much as 3.8% in Korean shares.

S&P 500 e-mini futures edged up 0.1%, while Japanese markets are closed for a holiday.

“Tuesday will be nothing more than the day ahead of a much bigger ​day,” ING analysts wrote in a note. By tomorrow, the market will have guidance on the midterm implications and the US Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcement, they ​wrote. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 2.1 basis points at 4.913%.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street edged ⁠lower, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.5% as tech sector earnings weighed on investor confidence, even as data showed US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid ​strong domestic demand.

Apple shares extended losses, falling 2.8% in after-hours trading after the iPhone maker on Monday forecast lower gross margins for the crucial holiday quarter, citing rising ​memory-chip costs, and projected services revenue growth that fell well short of Wall Street expectations.

Investors are also preparing to vote in the US midterm elections, where President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is facing a challenge to keep its hold on Congress.

Opinion polls favor the Democrats to win the House, though the Senate remains too close to call. Prediction market sites Polymarket and Kalshi currently ​assign around a 75% probability that the Democrats will control the Senate.

“Prediction markets imply the greatest likelihood of a Democratic ‘sweep’, but polling margins remain broadly comparable ​to Trump 1.0 midterms in 2018 when Democrats won the House decisively, but Republicans held onto the Senate,” MUFG analysts wrote in a note.

“Brazil’s election surprise is a reminder that prediction ‌markets can ⁠misprice political tail risks, raising questions around the roughly 70% odds now assigned to a blue ‘sweep’ in the midterms.”

Crude stabilises

Oil prices steadied after a fall, with Brent crude fluctuating between gains and losses and last 0.1% lower at $104.72 as trading resumed in Asia and investors weighed the state of peace talks between the US and Iran. The Wall Street Journal on Monday reported the US military struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, citing US officials.

Crude prices fell more than 7% on ​Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari ​officials lifted hopes for an end ⁠to the US-Israeli war with Iran and stabilisation of Middle East crude supply. “Oil prices fell sharply as renewed hopes for US-Iran diplomacy saw some geopolitical risk premium unwind,” Westpac analysts wrote.

In Asia-Pacific, Australian shares were up 0.1% and the Aussie dollar ​held steady at $0.70 ahead of the latest decision from the Reserve Bank of Australia, at which the central bank is widely ​expected to hike ⁠its cash rate target by 25 basis points to a near two-decade high of 4.85% from the current 4.6%.

Taiwanese shares fell 1.3%, while in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index was up 0.3%.

Against the Chinese yuan , the US dollar was 0.3% stronger at 6.6645 yuan in offshore trade after the People’s Bank of China said on Tuesday it ⁠would raise ​the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions to 6% from 4% from November 15.

The US ​dollar index , which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, edged up 0.1% to 101.81, recovering from a one-month low after slipping 0.2% on Monday.

Cryptocurrencies remained choppy after last week’s Binance ​hack, as customers withdrew a net $4.72 billion of funds. Bitcoin crawled 0.5% higher to $77,112.18 and ether nudged 0.1% lower to $2,253.59.

news.title: The Trump Era Marches On
news.text:
The headline from CNN was as basic as it was bold. It read: “Trump ramps up attacks on Democrats as ‘godless Communists’ ahead of November’s midterms.”

CNN reported as follows:

President Donald Trump on Friday seized on the electoral success of several democratic socialist candidates to ramp up his attacks on the Democratic Party, claiming it was being taken over by “godless Communists” who pose an existential threat to the nation.….“These are hard core, godless Communists,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post earlier on Friday, an accusation he repeated during remarks to a gathering of social conservatives. “This is the Greatest Threat to our Country since its Founding 250 years ago!”

Leave it to the plain-spoken president from the decidedly plain-spoken borough of Queens, New York City, to lay it on the line. There is no mistaking Trump’s point.

Which is, in short: That when an American political party from the Left ceases being a moderately left-mainstream Democrat in the tradition of Democrat heroes like FDR and JFK and instead goes full bore in a far-left direction, they should be called out for it. (RELATED: Paris Is Burning. Is Washington Next?)

In fact, no less than Ronald Reagan did exactly that in writing about the Democrats of his day. Writing this in his autobiography, Where’s the Rest of Me? (RELATED: Black Enthusiasm Gap Haunts Far Left Democrats)

Wrote the future president a couple of decades before becoming president in 1981:

Light was dawning in some obscure region in my head. I was beginning to see the seamy side of liberalism. Too many of the patches on the progressive coat were of a color I didn’t personally care for. Something the liberal will have to explain and stand trial for is his inability to see the Communist as he truly is and not as some kind of Peck’s Bad Boy of liberalism who is basically all right but just a bit overboard and rough-edged. This ideological myopia is even true of some who have met the Reds in philosophical combat and who should have learned something from crossing swords.

The interesting reality here is that Trump, like Reagan before him, has long ago come to realize that today’s Democrats have tilted so far left as to be around the political bend. And Trump today, like Reagan in his day, has not the least problem in bluntly calling them out.

There are, unsurprisingly, various milestones along the way of America’s political journey. Some may signal a conservative setback, others a conservative triumph.

Again, here is this regarding Trump:

President Donald Trump on Friday seized on the electoral success of several democratic socialist candidates to ramp up his attacks on the Democratic Party, claiming it was being taken over by “godless Communists” who pose an existential threat to the nation.

And again, there is this from Reagan years ago:

Light was dawning in some obscure region in my head. I was beginning to see the seamy side of liberalism. Too many of the patches on the progressive coat were of a color I didn’t personally care for. Something the liberal will have to explain and stand trial for is his inability to see the Communist as he truly is and not as some kind of Peck’s Bad Boy of liberalism who is basically all right but just a bit overboard and rough-edged.

The bottom line is clear. Both Reagan and Trump understood what was happening to the American Left of their day, and neither had the slightest hesitation in standing up and calling it out.

In today’s political world, Trump is doing for the country — whether the country yet realizes it or not — a huge political favor. Which is calling out the current American Left that has indeed become, in Trump’s words, “an existential threat to the nation.”

There were and are, both men believed, consequences for not speaking out against this. And in today’s world, the American people can be seriously grateful that President Trump recognizes the problem and refuses to be silent. Which is to say, the Trump era — like the Reagan era before it — marches on.

And an “Amen!” For that!

news.text: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who is accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston turned himself in Monday, his attorney said.Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. news.title: US lawmakers ask Trump administration to stop deportation of Afghans  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica News
news.text:
A group of 66 lawmakers in the United States has written to the administration of President Donald Trump asking it to halt a planned mass deportation of Afghans, including some who worked alongside coalition forces in Afghanistan before the military withdrawal in 2021.

In Monday’s letter, the lawmakers cited advocacy group reports that at least 150 Afghans were scheduled to be deported from Tuesday – flown from detention facilities in Louisiana to Pakistan.

The Associated Press news agency also reported that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials had said in court filings that they eventually planned on returning some of the Afghans to their home country.

The US does not have diplomatic relations with Afghanistan, which has been governed by the Taliban since US troops withdrew in August 2021.

“Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family’s suspected support of the US government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence,” the lawmakers wrote in the letter addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.

“Our country made a promise never to abandon the Afghans who sacrificed their own and their family’s safety to stand with American service members.”

Third-country deportations

As part of its crackdown on immigration, the Trump administration has made agreements with at least 35 countries to take in third-country nationals, in many cases because it cannot send them back to their home countries for fear they would be tortured, killed, or otherwise persecuted.

Critics of the practice have said it undermines decades of global humanitarian norms around asylum seeker and refugee protection. They say deportees often end up in countries with a record of human rights abuses, or places that are so dangerous the US tells its own citizens not to travel there.

The Trump administration has forcibly sent at least 25,000 people to third countries, according to a tally by nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First.

Human Rights First said it has confirmed that a flight carrying some of the Afghans from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan is scheduled for Tuesday.

Rights advocates say the batch of deportations to Pakistan may also include Iranians, small numbers of whom the Trump administration has previously sent to third countries to eventually be returned to Iran, despite the ongoing war the US is waging on the country.

Pakistan has deported millions of Afghans to Afghanistan in recent years, as relations with the Taliban have deteriorated.

Afghans in US left in limbo

Most of the Afghans scheduled for deportation did not have the opportunity to properly fight their removal in court, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the AfghanEvac advocacy group, said.

“They were placed into removal proceedings because they didn’t have attorneys to fight,” he said.

VanDiver said he spoke to one man on Monday, a former police officer in the Afghan government toppled by the Taliban, who expected to be deported and feared for his life if he ended up back in Afghanistan. Others, VanDiver said, had also either worked in the Afghan government or with the US, or had family that did so, and would be in danger in Afghanistan.

Since taking office, Trump has attempted to put an end to resettlement programmes for Afghans started by former President Joe Biden. More than 120,000 Afghans were evacuated from Afghanistan in 2021 after the chaotic withdrawal of US forces.

Some ended up in facilities abroad, like in Qatar. This September, the US granted a nine-month extension for Camp As Sayliyah, a facility in Qatar housing more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted US forces in Afghanistan.

Afghans evacuated to the US were initially granted humanitarian parole, allowing them to stay in the country. In 2022, the Biden administration granted them Temporary Protected Status for 18 months, allowing them to live and work legally in the US after their parole period expired, and while their immigration status was resolved.

But since then, few Afghans in the US have been able to move their applications for asylum, or other special protected status relating to their work with coalition forces, through the severely backlogged immigration system.

“These people are in dire straits; they have been stuck in this limbo for five years, waiting for permanency, waiting for green cards, waiting to hear about their status,” VanDiver said.

The Trump administration has instituted record-low quotas for asylum applications globally. However, he made an exception for white Afrikaners from South Africa, giving them sanctuary after alleging they had faced racial discrimination against white people.

Trump ordered a halt to processing applications from Afghans after a man from Afghanistan allegedly shot two National Guardsmen in Washington, DC, in November 2025. The Trump administration also included Afghan nationals in a blanket visa ban earlier this year, saying it would review immigration applications filed by anyone from the country. Both policies were challenged in court.

VanDiver said he and other advocates have been pushing for new legislation that would provide Afghans protection in the US, including a bill – co-sponsored by both Republican and Democratic lawmakers – that would grant many Temporary Protected Status after the Trump administration withdrew it.

news.title: Explosions hit Iran’s Qeshm Island as US media report US strikes in Hormuz  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily
news.text:
Several explosions have been heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island, as media outlets in the United States reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.

The blasts came in rapid succession late on Monday, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying in the sky over the island, which is located off Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz.

The semi-official Fars news agency said explosions were also heard in the port city of Bandar Lengeh, coming from the direction of the sea.

The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that the US military had carried out the strikes.

Some officials told the Journal the strikes were defensive, aimed at restricting Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. One official said the US had deliberately kept the campaign quiet to avoid signalling a return to major combat operations.

The Associated Press news agency also cited a US official as saying that the US had conducted defensive strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz. The official said “Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted.

Reporters with Fox News and Axios said the attacks were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing at a US aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Citing a US official, Fox News reporter Jennifer Griffin said the incident did not mark “the start of expanded strikes by the US”.

There was no immediate comment from authorities in Iran or the US.

Earlier on Monday, the IRGC had claimed it had captured two US reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm using electronic warfare systems and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The alleged US attacks come on the eve of crucial midterm elections, with US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party expected fighting to keep control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

They also came amid intensifying diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed US attacks on Iran.

news.title: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island ahead of crucial midterm elections
news.text: WASHINGTON: The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a US official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections.Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that "Iranians using surface to air missiles against US assets" had been targeted.The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the US would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on US gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.The region is on edge about the prospects of the US resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September, but thousands of US troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. Plus, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East.Before the strikes were confirmed, US Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal could still be struck. Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with "medical supplies and various things.""We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians," Vance told reporters Monday when asked about the letter. "I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We're going to keep on working at it.".US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after midterm elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about "the latest regional and international developments" and the Houthis' continued attacks on Saudi Arabia..Netanyahu is pressing Trump to attack Iran after the midterms, officials say.Trump says US still has to 'take care' of one or two targets in Iran.Trump downplays scale of Iran conflictOil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts in the Iran war appeared to show signs of headway.Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion."I don't know if you even call it a war, because we haven't been doing any fighting for months," Trump said.Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacyIran wants guarantees that the U.S. will implement its side of any agreement. The U.S. and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program..Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy.The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, met with Iran's military chiefs and said the response to "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without "geographic limits," urging an expansion of the list of potential targets.A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage.Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, told state television that "the tone has completely changed" from the U.S. and called it a "very good sign." He gave no details about the letter from Vance and said he had not responded..Iran warns of 'devastating' economic fallout from any new Israeli attack.Iran says in 'intensive' negotiations with US to avert war. Arab allies are caught in the middleOctober saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and "if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst."Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. news.title: An opening
news.text:
AS the threat of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran lingers, a parallel diplomatic process — facilitated by Qatar and Pakistan — is attempting to avert a devastating return to hostilities.

Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday to take part in indirect talks aimed at working out a deal, even as speculation of fresh attacks on Iran, following today’s midterm polls in America, continued.

US President Donald Trump has not helped matters by toying with the idea of new attacks. The ice was broken late last month when US Vice-President J.D. Vance wrote a letter to Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei.

Mr Vance reportedly prefers a diplomatic solution. Earlier, he had led his country’s delegation during April’s historic talks in Islamabad. The letter has been well received in Tehran, with Gen Rezaei calling its tone “positive”.

Writing to the Iranian security chief was an intelligent move and has begun to show results. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that if the US meets his country’s demands, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within two days. That outcome would be welcomed not only by the Gulf states and other regional countries but also by the international community at large, as states across the world have felt the impact of the strait’s closure and the attendant restrictions on trade and oil and gas flows.

Mr Vance’s letter has reportedly asked for guarantees regarding Iran’s nuclear programme. On its part, Tehran wants an end to both the sanctions and the US blockade, as well as other concessions from America.

Both sides must show flexibility if this push for peace is to succeed.

Though the diplomatic progress is welcome, the process could be torpedoed if the US and Israel go ahead with their attack plans. Media reports indicate that Washington and Tel Aviv are prepared to resume hostilities after the midterms. However, US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who has been briefed on the plans, has described the latter as “insane” and likely to cause a “devastating escalation”.

The Iranian Supreme Leader, on the other hand, has ordered his forces to retaliate to any attack “without geographical restriction”.

It would be very irresponsible of the US and Israel to scuttle peace efforts and spark a potentially massive conflict. The regional states do not want war as they are aware of the destruction it will bring. It is time for more mature officials within the US administration, such as Mr Vance, to take the lead in ensuring that the peace process continues unimpeded, while warmongers in America and Israel must be isolated.

If this brief opportunity for peace is wasted, sparking a wider conflict, the blame will rest squarely with the US president and the bloodthirsty Zionist regime.

Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

news.title: US midterms: Indian American candidates split final pitches between local issues, checking Trump
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 3 (IANS) Indian American candidates made sharply different closing arguments on the eve of Tuesday's US midterm elections, with Republicans pressing crime and living costs and Democrats casting the vote as a check on President Donald Trump and a stand against rising hate. In Ohio, Republican governor nominee Vivek Ramaswamy ended a statewide swing in Cleveland. "Slash property taxes quickly. Restore the rule of law on our streets. Cut electric bills by producing more energy. This isn't right vs. left. It's right vs. wrong. It's common sense vs. crazy. That's the choice tomorrow," he posted on X. "Ohioans first, that's my sole responsibility as Governor," he wrote after a stop in Toledo. In New York, Republican Saritha Komatireddy, who is challenging Attorney General Letitia James, toured Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Binghamton before a last stop on Long Island. "Crime, homelessness and fraud are all up under Letitia James, and she wouldn't change a thing. I'm the change New Yorkers have been waiting for," she posted. Komatireddy, the daughter of Indian immigrants, also tied her pitch to the immigrant story. Her campaign quoted her as saying: "You come to this country because there's a promise and a hope that if you work hard ... you can provide for yourself and your family." On the Democratic side, Congressman Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia framed the election around Trump. "Tomorrow we will elect a Congress that works for the people, not the President," he posted. Congressman Ro Khanna of California used the final weekend to push his Iran message. "Dems can vote to zero out appropriations for the war in Iran," he wrote, adding that Trump had called him "a lightweight 4 times". In Texas, Pooja Sethi, the Democratic candidate for state House District 47, closed on the anti-Indian hate that has shadowed the state's campaign. "We will not be intimidated. We will not be silenced. Hate has no home in Texas," she wrote. In Florida, Democrat Pia Dandiya, whose race in the 22nd Congressional District has drawn heavy outside spending, posted: "We have 1 day left to fight for a future worthy of our children." The split mirrors the national campaign, in which Republicans have stressed crime and prices while Democrats have focused on Trump, the Iran war and affordability.
